topic.name: Further Properties of Line Integrals of Scalar Functions

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=e^{2\theta}\,$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ shown above.
question.explanation:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C, $ i.e., \[ \int_C \,\textrm d s = L. \]

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

\[ \textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

\[ L= \int_C \,\textrm d s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

Since $r=e^{2\theta},$ we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2e^{2\theta}. \]

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: \begin{align*} \int_C \,\textrm d s &= \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\:\textrm{d}\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ \left(e^{2\theta}\right)^2 +\left(2e^{2\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ e^{4\theta} + 4e^{4\theta} }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ 5e^{4\theta} }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{5} \int_{0}^{\pi/2} e^{2\theta} \,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} e^{2\theta} \Bigr|_{0}^{\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} \left( e^{\pi} - e^{0} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} \left( e^{\pi} - 1 \right) \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1-\cos{\theta}}\,$ for $ -\dfrac{\pi}2 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}2$ ?
question.explanation:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C, $ i.e., \[ \int_C \,\textrm d s = L. \]

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

\[ \textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

\[ L= \int_C \,\textrm d s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

Since $r=\sqrt{1-\cos{\theta}}\,$ we have
\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = \dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{2\sqrt{1-\cos{\theta}}}. \]

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

\begin{align*} \int_C \,\textrm d s &= \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ \left(\sqrt{1-\cos{\theta}}\right)^2 +\left(\dfrac{\sin{\theta}}{2\sqrt{1-\cos{\theta}}}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ \left({1-\cos{\theta}}\right) +\dfrac{\sin^2{\theta}}{4({1-\cos{\theta}})} }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ \dfrac{4 (1-\cos{\theta}) ^2 +\left(1-\cos^2{\theta}\right)}{4(1-\cos{\theta})} }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ \dfrac{ (1-\cos{\theta}) \left( 4-4\cos \theta+1+\cos{\theta}\right)}{1-\cos{\theta}} }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ { 5-3\cos \theta} }\,\textrm{d}\theta \,. \end{align*}

question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\csc^3{\theta}\,$ for $\pi/3 \leq \theta \leq \pi/2?$
question.explanation:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C, $ i.e., \[ \int_C \,\textrm d s = L. \]

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

\[ \textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

\[ L= \int_C \,\textrm d s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

Since $r=\csc^3{\theta}\,$ we have
\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = -3\csc^3{\theta}\cot{\theta}. \]

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

\begin{align*} \int_C \,\textrm d s &= \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{ \left(\csc^3{\theta}\right)^2 +\left(-3\csc^3{\theta}\cot{\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{\csc^6{\theta}+9\csc^6{\theta}\cot^2{\theta} }\,\textrm{d}\theta\\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{\csc^6{\theta}(1+9\cot^2{\theta} })\,\textrm{d}\theta\\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2} \csc^3{\theta}\sqrt{1+9\cot^2{\theta} }\,\textrm{d}\theta \,. \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={\theta}^2\,$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq {\pi},$ shown above.
question.explanation:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C, $ i.e., \[ \int_C \,\textrm d s = L. \]

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

\[ \textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

\[ L= \int_C \,\textrm d s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

Since $r={\theta}^2,$ we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = {2\theta}. \]

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: \begin{align*} \int_C \,\textrm d s &= \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\:\textrm{d}\theta \\ &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{ \left(\theta^2\right)^2 +\left({2\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{ {\theta}^4 + 4{\theta}^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \sqrt{ \theta^2\left(4+\theta^2\right) }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} {\theta} \sqrt{4+\theta^2 } \,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 \int_{0}^{\pi} {2\theta} \sqrt{4+\theta^2 } \,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \left.\dfrac{ \left({4+\theta^2}\right)^{3/2}}3 \right|_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(\pi^2+4\right)^{3/2}-8}{3} \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves

question.text: Calculate $\displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r = 3\sin{\theta}\,$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ shown above.
question.explanation:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C, $ i.e., \[ \int_C \,\textrm d s = L. \]

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by \[ \textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have \[ L= \int_C \,\textrm d s = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta. \]

Since $r = 3\sin{\theta},$ we have \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 3\cos{\theta}. \]

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: \begin{align*} \int_C \,\textrm{d}s & = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\:\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \sqrt{ \left( 3\sin{\theta} \right)^2 + \left( 3\cos{\theta} \right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \sqrt{ 9\sin^2{\theta} + 9\cos^2{\theta} }\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \sqrt{9} \,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 3\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 3\theta \, \Big|_{0}^{\pi/4}\\[5pt] & = 3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 0 \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}. \end{align*}
